content: Additional therapies are recommended for children living with HIV who are also diagnosed with tuberculosis (TB) to improve TB treatment outcomes. These include co-trimoxazole preventive therapy (CPT), early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), pyridoxine supplementation, and nutritional support. Co-trimoxazole is a broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent that helps prevent secondary bacterial and parasitic infections in eligible children and adults with HIV. Daily CPT has been shown to prolong survival in children with HIV and reduce the incidence of co-morbidities, including co-infections like pneumocystis pneumonia in HIV-exposed infants. CPT is recommended for all HIV-exposed infants and children living with HIV, including those with TB, as part of a comprehensive HIV care package. Guidelines for initiating, discontinuing, and monitoring CPT are outlined in the 2006 WHO guidelines. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) in children with HIV aims to improve both the quality and length of life by reducing HIV-related morbidity and mortality. ART achieves this by decreasing the incidence of opportunistic infections (including TB), reducing viral load, restoring and preserving immune function, and supporting normal growth and development. ART has been shown to improve TB treatment outcomes in children with HIV. The WHO recommends ART for all individuals with confirmed HIV and a CD4 count of 500 cells/mm³ or less, prioritizing those with advanced HIV disease or a CD4 count of 350 cells/mm³ or less. ART is also recommended for individuals with active TB, hepatitis B virus (HBV) co-infection with severe liver disease, all pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV, all children under five years of age with HIV, and individuals in serodiscordant relationships, regardless of CD4 count. For children with active TB, TB treatment should be initiated first, followed by ART as soon as possible, ideally within eight weeks of starting TB treatment. For those with a CD4 count below 50 cells/mm³, ART should begin within two weeks of starting TB treatment. Simplified and less toxic ART regimens, preferably as fixed-dose combinations, are recommended for first-line therapy. For children older than three years, regimens typically include a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) backbone (e.g., tenofovir disoproxil fumarate [TDF] or abacavir [ABC] with lamivudine [3TC]) and a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) such as efavirenz (EFV). For children younger than three years, a protease inhibitor (PI)-based regimen combined with ABC or zidovudine (AZT) is preferred. ART regimens must be compatible with TB therapy, as drug interactions between rifampicin and certain ART drugs (e.g., lopinavir/ritonavir [LPV/r] or nevirapine [NVP]) can complicate co-treatment. In such cases, alternative regimens, such as triple NRTI therapy, may be considered. Adherence to ART in children presents unique challenges due to limited pediatric formulations, poor palatability of liquid medications, high pill or liquid volume burdens, large pill sizes, frequent dosing requirements, dietary restrictions, and potential adverse effects. Successful treatment requires the commitment of a responsible caregiver, who may also be living with HIV. Suboptimal care for caregivers can negatively impact the child’s treatment outcomes. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), sometimes referred to as a paradoxical reaction, may occur within three months of starting ART, most commonly within the first month. IRIS results from the restoration of cell-mediated immunity in response to mycobacterial antigens and can mimic worsening TB disease, presenting with fever, enlarged lymph nodes, or tuberculomas. Risk factors for IRIS include low baseline CD4 count, extensive TB disease, early ART initiation, and rapid immunological and virological responses to ART. While IRIS can cause significant morbidity, it is not associated with increased mortality. Anti-TB treatment should be continued in cases of TB-IRIS, and corticosteroids may be considered in some cases. For children with drug-resistant TB (DR-TB), including multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB), treatment follows the same principles as in adults, using second-line drugs. However, optimal treatment durations and regimens for children are not well established. Empirical treatment is often required when drug susceptibility testing (DST) is unavailable. Treatment regimens should include at least four effective drugs, guided by DST results from the child or the presumed source case. Preventive therapy for contacts of DR-TB patients is not currently recommended by WHO due to a lack of clinical trial data, although observational studies suggest that close contacts of DR-TB patients who develop TB disease often have drug-resistant disease. Children in contact with infectious TB cases should be screened for TB disease, with careful follow-up for asymptomatic children. If TB disease develops, treatment should be initiated based on the DST pattern of the presumed source case. In summary, managing TB and HIV co-infection in children requires a comprehensive approach, including early ART initiation, tailored drug regimens, and close monitoring for adherence and potential complications such as IRIS. For children with DR-TB, treatment regimens should be individualized based on DST results, and adherence to treatment principles is critical to achieving favorable outcomes.
